t:
For the purpose of this chapter—

    (1) 
“agency” means—

        (A) 
an Executive agency or part thereof;
 
        (B) 
an office or officer in the civil service or uni formed services in or under an Executive agency; and
 
        (C) 
the government of the District of Columbia or part thereof, except the courts;
   but does not include the General Accounting Office or the Comptroller General of the United States; and

    (2) 
“reorganization” means a transfer, consolidation, coordination, authorization, or abolition, referred to in section 903 of this title.

fable.w: This section only defines "agency" and "reorganization" for the executive reorganization chapter. The tempting reading is that the word "coordination" signals participation, but here it is just one type of reorganization of federal agencies, entirely inside the government. No outside party (states, the public, experts, companies) is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue over any federal decision.
fable.s: means a transfer, consolidation, coordination, authorization, or abolition, referred to in section 903 of this title

qwen_block.w: This section provides statutory definitions for the terms 'agency' and 'reorganization'. It does not establish any process for consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government. It merely defines the scope of entities considered agencies for the purposes of the chapter.
qwen_block.s: (1) “agency” means— (A) an Executive agency or part thereof; (B) an office or officer in the civil service or uni formed services in or under an Executive agency; and (C) the government of the District of Columbia or part thereof, except the courts; but does not include the General Accounting Office or the Comptroller General of the United States; and (2) “reorganization” means a transfer, consolidation, coordination, authorization, or abolition, referred to in section 903 of this title.

opus.w: This section only defines "agency" and "reorganization" for the executive reorganization chapter. It sets up no consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body, or right to sue. One might be tempted by the word "coordination" or by the mention of the District of Columbia government, which sits outside the federal government. But "coordination" here is one kind of reorganization, not consultation with outside parties. The District of Columbia is named only as an entity that can be reorganized, not as a participant in any federal decision.
opus.s: “reorganization” means a transfer, consolidation, coordination, authorization, or abolition, referred to in section 903 of this title.

qwen_chat.w: This section provides definitions for the terms 'agency' and 'reorganization' within the chapter. It does not establish any process for public comment, hearings, advisory committees with non-federal members, or consultation with outside entities before a federal decision is made. The inclusion of the District of Columbia government in the definition of 'agency' is a statutory classification for administrative purposes, not a requirement for participatory decision-making with external parties.
qwen_chat.s: For the purpose of this chapter— (1) “agency” means— (A) an Executive agency or part thereof; (B) an office or officer in the civil service or uni formed services in or under an Executive agency; and (C) the government of the District of Columbia or part thereof, except the courts; but does not include the General Accounting Office or the Comptroller General of the United States; and (2) “reorganization” means a transfer, consolidation, coordination, authorization, or abolition, referred to in section 903 of this title.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that defining "agency" to include the District of Columbia government implies some form of coordination or participation with a non-federal entity. However, this is merely a definitional section establishing the scope of terms for the chapter. It does not mandate any consultation, hearing, comment period, or advisory process involving outside parties. The District of Columbia government is treated as an "agency" for the purposes of this specific chapter's administrative procedures, but no interactive decision-making process with outsiders is described here.
